claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native oxide film formed under ambient conditions.
The native oxide scale initially protects pre-exposure Q235 steel.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between an oxide scale and its underlying material can generate high thermal stresses and exacerbate oxide spallation at elevated temperature.
Thermal cycling of Q235 steel produces repeated differential expansion and contraction between the oxide and steel substrate.
Repeated differential expansion under thermal cycling causes cumulative stress, microcracking, and eventual oxide detachment on Q235 steel.
Oxide microcracking and spallation compromise protective-film integrity and increase corrosion-related degradation.
Steady isothermal high-temperature exposure allows stress relaxation and more continuous oxide growth on Q235 steel.
Under isothermal high-temperature exposure, the Q235 oxide remains comparatively intact and maintains protection.
Under room-temperature conditions, the Q235 oxide remains comparatively intact and maintains protection.
A controlled comparison should expose identically prepared Q235 samples either isothermally at 700–900 °C or through cycles between room temperature and 700–900 °C in the same salt environment.
Thermally cycled samples will exhibit more oxide-scale spallation than isothermal high-temperature and room-temperature references.
Thermally cycled samples will exhibit higher mass loss than isothermal high-temperature and room-temperature references.
Thermally cycled samples will exhibit a greater microcrack density than isothermal high-temperature and room-temperature references.
Intermittent in situ stress-release or acoustic-emission events will coincide with oxide-fracture events.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily when significant temperature fluctuations occur.
The proposed mechanism may not govern under moderate or constant high-temperature conditions where stress relaxation occurs.
The proposed mechanism may not govern when salt-driven chemical reactions independently dominate oxide degradation.
Comparing thermal cycling in corrosive salt with thermal cycling in an inert atmosphere can help separate chemical effects from mechanically induced oxide disruption.
Failure to find statistically significant increases in microcracking, spallation, or mass loss relative to both isothermal and inert-atmosphere controls would reject the proposed governing mechanism.
